labs.outcome: Students relate interpretation to scientific explanation.
labs.understanding: Critical thinking supports valid interpretation of data.

K.text: Scientific explanations are based on observations and on interpretations of data.
Observation uses senses or tools to gather information.
Inference is an explanation based on observations and prior knowledge.
Both qualitative and quantitative data can support scientific explanations.

Critical-thinking skills involved in data interpretation include
• categorizing and recognizing patterns
• predicting outcomes
• analyzing relationships, e.g., cause and effect
• supporting or contradicting hypotheses
• justifying conclusions
Biases can influence the collection and interpretation of data.

Science-related careers apply interpretation and scientific explanation in areas such as
• mixtures and solutions, e.g., pharmacist
• structures and simple machines, e.g., structural engineer
• energy and heating, e.g., HVAC technician
• ecosystems, e.g., conservation biologist

S.text: Differentiate between observation and inference.
Interpret qualitative and quantitative data.
Discuss how predictions and hypotheses contribute to scientific explanations.
Develop a scientific explanation based on interpretation of data.
Discuss how bias can affect scientific explanations.
Explore how a science-related career applies interpretation and scientific explanation.

labs.title: Data Detective Lab

labs.outcome: Students analyze stability and biodiversity of ecosystems.
labs.understanding: The stability of ecosystems is influenced by biodiversity.

K.text: Ecosystems are dynamic and their characteristics can vary over time.

Components of ecosystems are interconnected with the following relationships:
• species, which are the same type of organism
• populations, which are interacting groups of the same species
• communities, which are interacting populations
• ecosystems, which are communities interacting with abiotic factors

Biodiversity refers to the variation
• within organisms of the same species (genetic diversity)
• in the number and abundance of different species (species diversity)
• in the number of unique habitat types in an ecosystem (ecosystem diversity)
Ecosystem stability is the capacity of an ecosystem to maintain its structure, biodiversity, and processes over time.
Each species in an ecosystem occupies an ecological niche, or role in their habitat, which allows different species to co-exist in the same environment.

Factors that influence a species’ ecological niche include
• biotic and abiotic factors
• adaptations
• competition
• predation
• symbiotic relationships
Adaptations are features that make a species well suited to a specific environment.
When species occupy distinct ecological niches, competition for resources is reduced.
Predation plays an important role in maintaining ecosystem stability.
Symbiotic relationships between different species include mutualism, commensalism, and parasitism.

S.text: Represent the interconnections between components within an ecosystem.
Investigate the biodiversity of species in various ecosystems.
Relate species adaptations to the environment in which species live.
Analyze the ecological niches of different species living in the same ecosystem.
Discuss how biodiversity supports ecosystem stability.

labs.title: Biodiversity and Stability Lab

labs.outcome: Students analyze stability and biodiversity of ecosystems.
labs.understanding: Ecosystem stability is maintained through the processes of cycling of matter and transfer of energy.

K.text: The continuous cycling of water through ecosystems supports life.

The continuous cycling of carbon includes
• photosynthesis
• respiration
• decomposition
• emission
• ocean exchange
• geological processes
The Sun is the primary source of energy in most ecosystems, and this energy is harnessed by producers.

Consumers can be classified according to trophic interactions as
• primary consumers
• secondary consumers
• tertiary consumers
• apex predators
Ecosystems have more producers than consumers because each time an organism is consumed, most of the energy from that organism is eventually transferred to the environment.
Food webs and energy pyramids can be used to represent the transfer of energy through trophic interactions among producers, consumers, and decomposers.

S.text: Discuss ways in which the water cycle supports life.
Represent how matter cycles within an ecosystem.
Represent energy transfer in an ecosystem, using an energy pyramid.
Analyze transfer of energy in trophic interactions.
Predict the effects of population change, including an extinction of species, on a food web.

labs.title: Energy Flow and Cycles Lab
review: LS2.K5: taught as more producer energy than consumer energy, since a pyramid of numbers can be inverted.
LS2.K4: apex predator taught as the top position in a chain, which can sit at any consumer level, not a fourth level after tertiary.
LS2.K3: chemosynthesis at deep-sea vents noted as the exception to Sun-powered ecosystems.

labs.outcome: Students analyze stability and biodiversity of ecosystems.
labs.understanding: Ecosystems can maintain stability despite disturbances.

K.text: Ecological succession is the predictable pattern of change in the types of species and habitat of an area when new areas become available for occupation (primary succession) or when existing areas undergo change (secondary succession).

Disturbances that can impact ecosystem stability include
• geological processes
• extreme weather events
• human activity
Biodiversity is declining on a global scale at an increasing rate due to habitat destruction, pollution, invasive species, and climate change.
Biodiversity can be reduced when species become endangered, extirpated, or extinct.

Caring for ecosystems is a shared responsibility that can involve collaboration, monitoring data, and interventions such as
• species relocation
• habitat conservation
• protecting water resources

Forest management supports ecosystem stability by using practices such as
• selective harvesting
• reduced impact logging
• reforestation
• controlled burning
• wildfire risk reduction

S.text: Explore how ecosystem stability can be disturbed.
Discuss factors that contribute to declining biodiversity in an ecosystem.
Describe ecological succession in ecosystems.
Discuss possible ways to care for an ecosystem.
Evaluate data collected from an ecosystem with decreasing biodiversity.

labs.title: Disturbance and Succession Lab
review: LS3.K1: succession taught as predictable in general pattern only (species and timing vary); secondary succession defined as following a disturbance that leaves soil, roots and seeds.
LS3.K3: overexploitation added once as a fifth global driver; Living Planet Index (73% since 1970, 2024) and IPBES (about one million species at risk) figures need a currency check.

LS3.K4: COSEWIC threatened and special concern categories added; species statuses (whooping crane, swift fox, greater sage-grouse, westslope cutthroat trout, greater prairie-chicken) need verification on the Species at Risk Public Registry.
LS3.K5: First Nations and Métis roles (bison restoration, Indigenous Guardian programs) described generally; please review wording and consider a community partner.
LS3.K6: controlled burning taught as planned fire by trained crews; Indigenous cultural burning intentionally not detailed.
LS3.S5: wetland monitoring data set is invented for practice and labelled as such; 2016 survey uses half effort to teach sampling bias.

labs.outcome: Students analyze pure substances and mixtures.
labs.understanding: Matter can be classified based on physical properties and separated according to its particles.

K.text: Matter can be classified as a pure substance or mixture.
A pure substance is composed of only one type of particle, and those particles cannot be separated by using physical techniques.

Pure substances can be identified or described by physical properties, including
• appearance, e.g., colour and lustre
• density
• freezing point
• melting point
• boiling point
Density is the mass per unit volume of a substance d = m/V
A mixture is composed of two or more types of particles, and those particles can be separated by using physical techniques.

Mixtures can be classified as
• heterogeneous, including mechanical mixtures
• homogeneous, including solutions

Techniques used to physically separate heterogeneous mixtures include
• mechanical separation, which is based on particle size and density, e.g., sorting, sieving, and filtration
• magnetic separation, which is based on magnetism
Distillation is a technique used to physically separate homogeneous mixtures based on boiling points.

S.text: Investigate physical properties of various pure substances.
Represent the particle composition of pure substances and mixtures.
Solve problems involving calculations related to density when given mass and volume.
Classify pure substances and mixtures.
Separate mixtures according to physical properties.

refs.title: Mix and Flow of Matter: Interactive Study Lab

labs.title: Matter Sorter Lab
review: M1.K2: 'one type of particle' taught precisely as one kind of atom (element) or one kind of joined-atom particle (compound); compounds noted as separable only by chemical change.
M1.K3: melting and freezing point taught as the same temperature for a pure substance; mixtures melt or boil over a range; boiling points at sea level (water about 98 °C in Edmonton).

M1.K6/K7: mechanical mixture taught as heterogeneous with visible parts, suspensions included; density methods (settling, decanting, panning, flotation) grouped under mechanical separation with density named.
M1.K8: distillation taught for salt water and for water and ethanol; one distillation of ethanol and water gives a richer mixture, not pure ethanol; evaporation not taught separately.

M1: Alberta examples (oil sands hot-water extraction, Edmonton-area refineries, river water treatment, recycling magnets) described generally; property values are rounded reference values; mystery samples are practice data.

labs.outcome: Students analyze pure substances and mixtures.
labs.understanding: Particles can interact to form solutions.

K.text: A solution is a homogeneous mixture in which solute particles dissolve in a solvent.
Dissolving is the process by which particles of solute become evenly distributed among particles of a solvent.
Stirring or increasing the solute’s surface area can increase the rate of dissolving.
Solutions can be described by their concentration, including dilute or saturated.
Solubility is a physical property that describes the amount of solute that can be dissolved in a given amount of solvent at a specific temperature.
The amount of solute that dissolves in a specific amount of solvent can increase as the solvent’s temperature increases.

S.text: Relate solubility, concentration, and dissolving.
Represent various concentrations of solutions.
Investigate factors that influence solubility.

refs.title: Mix and Flow of Matter: Interactive Study Lab

labs.title: Solution Mixer Lab
review: M2.K4: 'dilute or saturated' taught as two separate scales (dilute/concentrated for amount dissolved; unsaturated/saturated for whether more can dissolve); a saturated solution of a barely soluble solute is still dilute.
M2.K6: 'can increase' taught as true for most solids; table salt barely changes, and gases (oxygen, carbon dioxide) become less soluble as water warms; crystallization added as context.
M2.K5: solubility values are rounded reference values in g per 100 g water (salt 36.0, potassium nitrate 31.6, sucrose about 204, baking soda 9.6 at 20 °C; oxygen about 9.1 mg/L); please spot check.
M2.K3: warming mentioned once as another way to speed dissolving (draft lists only stirring and surface area); M2.K2 adds dissolving is not melting and mass is conserved.

M2: Alberta examples (Fort Saskatchewan salt caverns by solution mining, Edmonton road brine, trout and cold water) described generally; Lab Bench solubility data and dissolving race times are simulated practice data.

labs.outcome: Students investigate the relationships between energy, temperature, and heating.
labs.understanding: Transfer of energy can be used to explain change in objects and systems.

K.text: In science, energy is a quantity, not a physical substance, that is measured in joules, which indicates the amount of work that can be done on an object or in a system.
A system can be described in terms of its components and their interactions, while the surroundings are everything outside of the system.
The transfer of energy drives change, and changes in an object or system indicate that work has been done.
The total change in a system’s energy is equal to the total amount of energy that transfers into or out of the system.

S.text: Illustrate the transfer of energy into, within, and out of a system.
Analyze changes in energy when work is done.

labs.title: Energy Accounts Lab
review: EN1.K1: 'indicates the amount of work that can be done' taught as a helpful description; strictly, energy is the capacity to do work or to heat, and not all of a system's energy can become work.
EN1.K3: 'changes indicate that work has been done' taught as changes showing that energy was transferred, by work or by heating, so EN2 is not contradicted; pushing without movement does no work.
EN1.K3/S2: W = F × d borrowed from F2.K2 as context; for lifting, force equals weight (about 9.8 N per kg); energy stores not listed (Science 8).

EN1: joule ladder values are rounded estimates (1 L of water to boiling about 335 kJ, 100 food Calories about 420 kJ, 1 kWh = 3.6 MJ); transfer diagram numbers, bouncing ball data and practice problems are made up and labelled.

labs.outcome: Students investigate the relationships between energy, temperature, and heating.
labs.understanding: Objects or systems experience temperature changes because of energy transfer.

K.text: Temperature is a measure of the average energy of motion of the particles in an object or a system and can be used to describe hotness or coldness.
The faster the particles in an object or system move, the greater their average energy of motion and the higher the temperature.
Heating is the transfer of energy that occurs from a higher-temperature object or system to a lower-temperature object or system.

Heating occurs through the processes of
• conduction
• convection
• radiation

Conduction, convection, and radiation can be used in technologies, such as
• electric stoves, which use conduction
• hot-air balloons, which use convection
• microwave ovens, which use radiation

Insulation is used to slow rates of heat transfer and can be found in systems such as
• nature, e.g., whale blubber
• technologies, e.g., cooler
Some of the radiation from the Sun and from space is reflected or absorbed by Earth’s atmosphere and surface.
Most energy absorbed by Earth’s surface eventually radiates back up, contributing to further absorption and reflection in the atmosphere.
The absorption and reflection of radiation by Earth’s atmosphere and surface affect the temperature of Earth.

S.text: Explain how heating occurs through conduction, convection, and radiation.
Discuss how the processes of conduction, convection, or radiation are used in various technologies.
Investigate systems that minimize energy transfer.
Describe how Earth’s temperature is affected by radiation from the Sun.

labs.title: Temperature and Heating Lab
review: EN2.K1: temperature taught as average energy of motion, kept separate from total energy (warm bathtub vs hot cocoa); Kelvin not named; particle animation exaggerates speed change, readout uses square-root relationship.

EN2.K3: heating taught as spontaneous from hotter to colder until thermal equilibrium; cold does not flow; fridges and heat pumps noted as using work; mixing-water weighted average added as a worked example (no energy lost).

EN2.K5: electric coil also radiates but contact conduction taught as main; hot-air balloon taught as heated air becoming less dense and rising (same idea as convection); microwaves absorbed mainly by water, then conduction spreads energy inward.
EN2.K8: surface taught as giving energy back mostly as infrared, with evaporation and rising warm air also named; greenhouse gases (water vapour, carbon dioxide) absorb and send some back down.

EN2.K7/K9/S4: energy budget rounded to about 30 reflected, 20 absorbed by atmosphere, 50 by surface; Earth's thermostat is a one-layer model (about −18 °C without greenhouse effect, about 15 °C today); cocoa cooling data and reflection values are made up or rounded for practice.

labs.outcome: Students investigate the interactions of forces applied to structures and simple machines.
labs.understanding: Structures can be designed and constructed to withstand different types of forces.

K.text: Structures are composed of interacting components, such as beams, columns, and arches.
Natural structures can inspire the design and construction of human-made structures.

Loads are forces that act on structures and can be classified as
• permanent, e.g., weight of the structure
• non-permanent, e.g., wind, weight of snow, weight of occupants, and ground shifting
Structural deformation from internal forces, external forces, or both can cause changes to a structure’s shape or integrity.
Structural fatigue is progressive damage from repeated or cyclic loading that can lead to a structure’s failure over time.

Structural deformation and failure can result from
• flawed design
• poor construction
• improper load
• structural fatigue

Factors that can affect the design and construction of structures include
• function
• available resources
• safety
• intended lifespan and sustainability

Natural and constructed structures can be categorized as
• mass or solid
• frame
• shell
Structures from different categories can be combined to better withstand a load.

S.text: Develop a structure that supports a load.
Identify the components and categories of a structure.
Classify loads as permanent or non-permanent.
Compare natural structures to human-made structures.
Investigate a structure failure.
Compare the effectiveness of structures that have a common function but different designs.

labs.title: Structures and Loads Lab
review: F1.K3: permanent loads linked to dead load and non-permanent to live and environmental loads; snow densities (about 100, 300, 450 kg/m³) and W = m × 9.8 N/kg are rounded context values.
F1.K4: internal forces defined as compression, tension, shear and torsion with bending as compression plus tension; external forces as loads; elastic vs permanent deformation added.
F1.K5: fatigue taught as cracks growing a little each cycle under loads below the one-time breaking load; paper clip cycle counts are made up.

F1.K6/S5: Quebec Bridge (1907) and Tacoma Narrows (1940) summaries need verification; Iron Ring mentioned only as often linked to Quebec Bridge; worker deaths are a sensitive topic; four other case files are invented practice.
F1.K8/K9: mass taught as the same as solid; tipi (frame of poles with a cover) and Inuit snow house (dome-shaped shell) described generally; please review wording and consider a community partner.
F1.S1/S6: craft stick bridge strengths are a made-up model (about 10% random variation); efficiency (load held ÷ mass) added to compare designs.

labs.outcome: Students investigate the interactions of forces applied to structures and simple machines.
labs.understanding: Machines can change the force required to complete a task.

K.text: Force, expressed in newtons, has both magnitude and direction.
Work, expressed in joules, is done when an applied force moves an object a distance in the direction of the force W =F ×d.

Simple machines can accomplish a task by changing the magnitude or direction of the input force and include
• inclined planes
• levers
• wheels and axles
• screws
• wedges
• pulleys
In a simple machine, the input work is equal to the output work.
Mechanical advantage occurs when a machine reduces the input force needed to move an object by increasing the distance over which the force is applied.
Complex machines, such as a wheelbarrow or a can opener, are made by combining simple machines.
A complex machine’s mechanical advantage is the product of the mechanical advantages of the simple machines.

S.text: Analyze work done in a local setting involving simple machines.
Explain the relationship between work, force, and distance.
Solve problems involving calculations related to work when given force and distance.
Explain why the amount of work does not change when a simple machine is used.
Compare the mechanical advantage of various simple and complex machines.

labs.title: Machines and Work Lab
review: F2.K4: input work = output work taught as true for an ideal (frictionless) machine; real machines put out slightly less work, efficiency = output ÷ input × 100% added.
F2.K5: MA defined as output force ÷ input force (ideal MA = input distance ÷ output distance); fixed pulley MA 1 (direction only) and tools with MA below 1 (canoe paddle, snow shovel) noted.
F2.K7: product rule taught for machines linked in a chain; wheelbarrow's wheel mainly reduces rolling friction, so its MA comes mainly from the lever; chain and comparison MA values are made up.
F2.K2: work counts only distance moved in the direction of the force; carrying a box at constant height does no work by the holding force; W = m × 9.8 N/kg weight added as context (F2.K1).
F2.S1: local sites (school flagpole, entrance ramp, garden wheelbarrow, oil field pump jack, canoe loading) use made-up numbers; ramp trial data are simulated with friction.

labs.outcome: Students examine how design processes can be used to arrive at solutions.
labs.understanding: Design processes can be used to solve problems.

K.text: Design thinking is an innovative approach to solving problems.

Design processes are iterative, often collaborative, and include
• identifying the problem
• researching
• brainstorming solutions
• planning and developing a prototype
• testing and refining
Solutions can address needs, wants, or problems and can be products, processes, or services.

Design processes can be supported by computational thinking, which includes
• decomposition
• pattern recognition
• abstraction
• algorithms
User interaction, such as a user interface, should be considered when designing solutions.
Universal design considers users’ diverse needs and abilities and can support design processes and accessibility.

S.text: Solve a problem, using design processes.
Discuss solutions that incorporate universal design.
Evaluate the use of universal design in a user interaction.

labs.title: Design Process Studio Lab
review: CS3.K1: design thinking taught as a human-centred approach starting with empathy and a 'How might we' question; 'innovative' explained as leading to new ideas, not the only innovative method.

CS3.K2: the five draft steps taught as one common version of a design process (others exist, e.g., empathize, define, ideate, prototype, test); iteration taught as looping back to any earlier step, not only to refine.
CS3.K3: needs/wants/problems and products/processes/services taught as overlapping labels; need defined as required to be safe, healthy or able to take part.

CS3.K6: Ronald Mace credited with popularizing 'universal design' in the 1980s and the seven principles to the Center for Universal Design (NC State, 1997); please verify. UDL noted as related but not taught; disability wording needs review.
CS3: boot room survey, prototype tester model, user personas, decision matrix and audit scenarios are made up for practice and labelled.

labs.outcome: Students explore ways to communicate with computer systems.
labs.understanding: Computers use programs to perform tasks.

K.text: A program is a set of instructions written in a programming language that a computer can run to perform tasks.
Decomposition is the process of breaking a task into smaller parts, which can be accomplished by using functions.
Functions are organized blocks of code designed to perform specific tasks within a program.

Most programming languages include built-in functions for common tasks, such as
• draw
• add
• print
• move

A function has a descriptive name, inputs, an algorithm, and an output and can be used within
• sequences
• loops
• conditionals, e.g., if–then–else
The input–process–output, or IPO, cycle is a model describing how computer systems use hardware and software to input data, process it, and generate output.
Software consists of code that instructs hardware, the physical components of a computer.

Types of software include
• system software, e.g., operating systems that enable users to efficiently operate a computer
• programming software, e.g., tools that help programmers code
• application software, e.g., word processing or data processing programs

An interface is a device or program that can enable communication between
• software and hardware, e.g., printer driver
• user and computer, e.g., touch screen

S.text: Decompose a larger task into smaller tasks.
Explain a built-in function within a sequence of visual block-based code.
Create a sequence using various built-in functions within visual block-based code.
Compare two or more sequences with different functions that achieve the same result.
Discuss potential improvements to existing code.
Model the IPO cycle.
Explore various configurations of hardware and software.

labs.title: Programs and Instructions Lab
review: CS1.K1: taught that code is translated (compiled or interpreted) into machine instructions before the processor runs it; the 'processor view' binary in Lesson 1 is an illustration only.

CS1.K4: draw, add, print and move taught as common built-in jobs whose names vary by language (Scratch uses pen blocks and an operator block for adding; Python usually uses +); the lab's turtle uses the four names as listed.

CS1.K5: four parts of a function taught with the precision that some functions take no inputs (turnRight()) and some cause an action instead of returning a value (drawSquare()); inputs also called parameters.

CS1.K6: IPO taught as a cycle where output leads to new input; storage mentioned once (input–process–output–storage model); thermostat, self-checkout, bus fare card reader and game controller described generally.
CS1.K8: software types taught as overlapping groups; Windows, macOS, ChromeOS, Android and iOS named as common examples only.

CS1.K9: driver taught as software linking the OS and apps to one hardware model; touch screen as hardware in a user interface; Canadian French and Cree syllabics keyboard layouts mentioned once as interface settings, please review wording.
CS1: trace programs are randomized practice; configuration jobs, IPO systems and code review cases are made up and labelled.

labs.outcome: Students explore ways to communicate with computer systems.
labs.understanding: Machines can learn to perform tasks.

K.text: Artificial intelligence, or AI, can be defined as the ability of a machine to adapt its action in response to received data, prior interactions, and its environment.

Machine learning is a type of AI that is trained from data and can
• identify patterns
• make predictions or decisions
• improve performance over time without additional programming
• adapt based on input from new data
Narrow AI is designed to perform specific tasks, such as voice recognition or running recommendation algorithms.
General AI is designed to display human-like intelligence, reasoning, and adaptability across a wide range of tasks.

S.text: Determine whether a digital technology uses AI.
Discuss how AI differs from other computer programs.
Explore the role of data in machine learning.
Compare narrow AI and general AI.

labs.title: Learning Machines Lab
review: CS2.K1: draft AI definition is broad (a simple thermostat also responds to environmental data); taught as a machine changing its own behaviour from data and experience beyond fixed human-written rules; definitions vary.
CS2.K2: 'without additional programming' taught as without a programmer writing new rules; people still collect data and retrain, and many deployed models only improve when retrained.
CS2.K3: Chinook (University of Alberta checkers program, could not be beaten) and Amii (Alberta Machine Intelligence Institute, Edmonton) named as local context; please verify wording.

CS2.K4: general AI taught as a goal no system is widely accepted as reaching, with experts disagreeing on whether or when; chatbots noted as harder to classify; fast-changing, re-check before teaching.
CS2.S3: bias in data, wrong labels and data drift added to explain the role of data; k-nearest-neighbour sorter, bird call scores, spam messages, books and accuracy results are made up for practice.

labs.outcome: Students investigate natural phenomena in relation to interactions of celestial bodies.
labs.understanding: Interactions of celestial bodies are observed and experienced on Earth.

K.text: Natural phenomena that result from interactions of celestial bodies include tides, eclipses, and lunar phases.
Tides result from gravitational forces of the Sun and the Moon.
A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes between Earth and the Sun, casting a shadow on a small portion of Earth, totally or partially blocking the view of the Sun from that area.
A total or partial lunar eclipse occurs when Earth is directly between the Moon and the Sun, resulting in Earth casting a shadow on the Moon.

Lunar phases are observed changes in the illumination of the Moon as a result of cyclical patterns in the Moon’s orbit and include
• new moon
• first quarter moon
• full moon
• last quarter moon

S.text: Discuss tides in relation to gravitational forces.
Explain lunar and solar eclipses in relation to the position of Earth, the Moon, and the Sun.
Represent lunar phases.

labs.title: Moon and Tides Lab
review: SP1.K2: tides taught as caused by the difference in the Moon’s and Sun’s pull across Earth (two bulges); Sun’s tidal effect about half the Moon’s; spring and neap tides, about two high tides every 24 h 50 min, and coastline effects (Bay of Fundy up to about 16 m, needs a spot check) added as context.

SP1.K3: umbra (total) and penumbra (partial) named; path of totality usually under about 270 km wide; annular eclipses added in Lab Bench 4 with rounded apparent-size values; April 8, 2024 eclipse route through Ontario, Quebec and Atlantic Canada needs a spot check; eye safety stressed.
SP1.K4: 'directly between' taught as a close line-up at full moon; red colour explained by sunlight bent and filtered through Earth’s air; penumbral stage shown only as faint dimming.

SP1.K5: four listed phases taught as main phases with crescent and gibbous added; 'cyclical patterns in the Moon’s orbit' taught as the changing Sun-Earth-Moon angle over about 29.5 days; Earth’s-shadow misconception addressed; Northern Hemisphere view.
SP1.K3/K4: Moon’s 5° orbit tilt and eclipse seasons added to explain why eclipses are not monthly; tilt model exaggerated.

SP1.K5: Lesson 2 says in general terms that First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples have long followed the Moon’s cycle; no specific community knowledge; please review wording and consider a Knowledge Keeper.
SP1.S1: Practice Harbour tide data are made up (smooth 12.42 h model) and labelled; diagrams not to scale.

labs.outcome: Students investigate natural phenomena in relation to interactions of celestial bodies.
labs.understanding: Celestial bodies move in predictable patterns.

K.text: Gravity, an attractive force between objects, can cause celestial bodies to orbit each other.
Models can be used to represent movement patterns and distances between celestial bodies.
Geocentric models of the solar system were used to explain the motion of the planets until evidence supported the heliocentric model.
Solar systems exist on large scales and are measured in astronomical units, or AU.

S.text: Compare geocentric and heliocentric models of the solar system.
Explore a scale model of our solar system.
Describe movement patterns of and distances between celestial bodies in the heliocentric model of the solar system.

labs.title: Solar System Patterns Lab
review: SP2.K1: orbit taught as gravity plus sideways motion (gravity alone would pull bodies together); shared balance point (Earth and Moon about 4700 km from Earth’s centre) added; Newton’s cannon speeds (about 7.9 and 11.2 km/s) rounded, mountain not to scale.

SP2.K3: change taught as gradual (Copernicus 1543 to Bessel’s parallax 1838); Venus phases ruled out Ptolemy’s model but not Tycho’s hybrid, so Kepler and Newton included; epicycle model simplified (no equant).

SP2.K3: worldwide contributions (Aristarchus, Ptolemy, Aryabhata, al-Tusi, Ibn al-Shatir, Copernicus, Tycho, Galileo, Kepler, Newton, Bessel) summarized with approximate dates; please spot check wording and dates.

SP2.K4: ‘solar systems’ taught as planetary systems around other stars (ours is the solar system); AU rounded to 150 million km (defined as 149 597 870 700 m); light-year (about 63 000 AU) added as context.
SP2.S3: planet distances, periods, speeds and diameters are rounded reference values; Kepler’s rule P² = a³ shown as context only; orrery squeezes orbits and uses made-up starting positions.
SP2.S2: scale model values calculated in the page; Proxima Centauri (about 268 000 AU), Edmonton to Calgary (about 300 km) and the Beaver Hills Dark Sky Preserve planet note are rounded or general.

labs.outcome: Students examine how geological processes continually reshape Earth’s surface.
labs.understanding: Earth’s surface is constantly changing due to the dynamic interactions of various geological processes.

K.text: Earth is a dynamic planet that is shaped by internal and external geological processes.
Hydrological processes, such as wave action, glacial processes, and groundwater flow, contribute to geological processes.
The geological processes of weathering, erosion, transport, and deposition change Earth’s surface.
Earth’s crust is composed of rocks and minerals.
Weathering, which can be physical, chemical, or biological, breaks down rocks and minerals into sediments.

Erosion removes and transports weathered sediments and debris, creating features
• on Earth’s surface, e.g., hoodoos
• beneath Earth’s surface, e.g., caves

Erosion is influenced by many factors, including
• weather and climate
• hydrological processes
• features of the land (topography)
• vegetation cover
• human activities
Mass wasting is a type of erosion in which rocks, soil, or debris move downhill because of gravity, e.g., landslides and rockfalls.

Mass wasting can be triggered by many factors, including
• water
• earthquakes
• human activity
Deposition occurs when sediments are transported by wind, water, or ice and are dropped in a new location, resulting in landforms such as deltas and dunes.

S.text: Describe local areas that have experienced weathering and erosion.
Explain how geological processes change Earth’s surface.
Investigate the relationship among various geological processes.
Discuss the impact of mass-wasting events that have occurred in Alberta.
Suggest solutions to minimize the impact of potential mass-wasting events.

labs.title: Weathering and Erosion Lab
review: ES1.K1: internal processes taught as powered by Earth's inner heat (build up land) and external as powered by the Sun and gravity (wear down land); plate tectonics left to Science 9.

ES1.K2: running water in rivers added briefly beside wave action, glacial processes and groundwater; Big Rock described as an erratic from the Jasper area and the Blackfoot origin of the name Okotoks mentioned once; please review.
ES1.K3/K6: transport kept as a separate step from erosion to match the draft (many geologists include it in erosion); Drumheller hoodoo cap rock and Rat's Nest Cave descriptions need verification.
ES1.K8: mass wasting taught as a type of erosion as drafted (some texts treat it separately); slump, debris flow and creep added.

ES1.S4: Frank Slide facts (April 29, 1903; about 110 million tonnes; about 100 seconds; at least 70 deaths; Alberta Geological Survey monitoring), Cougar Creek 2013, Edmonton river valley slumps and Peace River landslides summarized generally and need verification; deaths and flood losses are sensitive.

ES1.K10: Peace-Athabasca Delta (one of the largest freshwater deltas), Middle Sand Hills dunes and river speed thresholds need a check; erosion index, test tray data and slope factor of safety model are made up for practice and labelled.

labs.outcome: Students examine how geological processes continually reshape Earth’s surface.
labs.understanding: Transformation of rock through the rock cycle results from geological processes.

K.text: Rocks are formed, broken down, and reformed through specific processes on or below Earth’s surface, which occur at different rates and are referred to as the rock cycle.

Rocks are classified as sedimentary, igneous, or metamorphic according to how they were formed and their characteristics, including
• texture
• layering
• mineral composition
Sedimentary rock is formed on or just below Earth’s surface through compaction and cementation of sediments.
Igneous rock is formed on or below Earth’s surface through cooling and crystallization of molten rock, including magma or lava.
Metamorphic rock is formed below Earth’s surface through extreme heat and pressure acting on pre-existing rocks.
Common minerals found in rock include quartz, feldspar, mica, and calcite.
Minerals can be identified by properties such as colour, lustre, streak, transparency, hardness, and magnetism.

S.text: Explain the rock cycle.
Analyze characteristics of local rocks.
Classify rocks as sedimentary, igneous, or metamorphic.
Investigate how different types of rocks were formed.
Identify different minerals from a sample.

labs.title: Rock Cycle Lab
review: ES2.K1: rock cycle taught as many possible paths (shortcuts such as igneous to metamorphic shown), not a fixed loop; process times are rough rounded ranges on a log timeline.
ES2.K3: sediment defined to include shells and plant remains so limestone and coal fit; rocks that crystallize out of water (rock salt) not taught.
ES2.K4: intrusive and extrusive added; obsidian taught as glass with no crystals, so crystallization happens only when there is time for it.
ES2.K5: 'extreme heat and pressure' taught as enough to change minerals while the rock stays solid; melting makes magma; contact metamorphism not named.
ES2.K6: mica and feldspar taught as mineral groups (biotite, muscovite named); calcite taught as the main mineral of limestone and marble, not granite.

ES2.S4: cooling investigation crystal sizes and rock clock deposition rates are made up for practice and labelled.

labs.outcome: Students examine how geological processes continually reshape Earth’s surface.
labs.understanding: Geological processes and human activity can affect the nature of soil.

K.text: Soil is a thin layer of minerals and organic matter, formed over time through weathering, erosion, and decomposition.

There are various types of soil, e.g., sand, clay, and loam, which can be described based on physical properties, including
• composition
• colour
• odour
• pore size

Factors that affect the nature of soil include
• parent material
• climate
• biotic components
Healthy soil is a complex mixture of components, including organic matter, oxygen, carbon dioxide, minerals, water, nutrients, and biodiverse organisms.

Healthy soil improves
• food security
• climate resilience
• nutrient cycling
• air and water quality
• biodiversity
• sustainable agricultural systems

Humans can improve soil health and reduce erosion in a variety of ways, such as
• planting cover crops
• mulching
• practising conservation tillage
• using buffer strips
• using controlled burning
• practising rotational grazing

S.text: Design and conduct a controlled experiment to determine how different types of soil affect plant growth.
Describe factors that affect the nature of soil.
Explain how a given component of healthy soil leads to related improvements.
Discuss the impact of human activity on local soil health.

labs.title: Soil Health Lab
review: ES3.K1: 'thin layer' shown as under 2 m with an apple peel comparison; formation rate given only as 'hundreds of years or more' for a few centimetres; O, A, B, C and bedrock layers added as context.

ES3.K2: silt added as the third particle size so loam can be defined (sand 0.05 to 2 mm, silt 0.002 to 0.05 mm, clay under 0.002 mm); jar test uses a simplified soil type rule, not the full texture triangle.

labs.outcome: Students examine environmental stewardship.
labs.understanding: Environmental stewardship can address present needs that consider the environment and human well-being.

K.text: Environmental stewardship refers to the shared responsibility of individuals and groups at local, provincial, national, and international levels to protect, restore, and sustainably use the environment and its resources.

The protection, restoration, and sustainable use of the environment and its resources can be accomplished through actions such as
• the creation and maintenance of protected areas to conserve biodiversity
• waste reduction and circular economy practices
• responsible water management and conservation
• the reintroduction of native species

A circular economy is a way of designing and using products so that materials are reused, repaired, or recycled instead of being thrown away, helping to reduce waste and protect the environment, e.g., clothing rental and resale programs.
Benefits of environmental stewardship include enhanced ecosystem stability and improved human well-being.

Environmental stewardship efforts can be motivated by
• desire to take care of the environment for future generations
• monetary incentives
• government regulations

S.text: Explore motivations that inspire environmental stewardship.
Research an action that promotes environmental stewardship.
Create a plan for engaging in environmental stewardship at home or at school.
Investigate how a circular economy contributes to environmental stewardship.
Explain the similarities and differences between protecting and caring for something and owning something.

labs.title: Stewardship Action Lab
review: SL2.K3: circular economy taught with loops in order of value (keep using, share or rent, repair, resell, recycle last); recycling described as taking energy and often lowering quality; 'design' added as the first step; jacket loop numbers are made up.

SL2.K1/K2: examples need a currency check: Banff plains bison from Elk Island (2017), swift fox reintroduction from the 1980s (now threatened), Elk Island bison conservation, Alberta container deposit, Edmonton waste sorting, Migratory Birds Convention (1916), Montreal Protocol (1987), Canada's 30 by 30 goal under the Kunming-Montreal framework (2022).
SL2.K4: human well-being benefits described generally, with no health statistics.
SL2.K5: motivations taught as usually mixed; regulation examples (Species at Risk Act, city waste rules, water licences) described generally.

SL2.S5: Treaty 6 note describes First Nations and Métis relationships with land generally (responsibility rather than ownership); please review wording and consider a Knowledge Keeper; 'most of Alberta's land is public (Crown) land' needs checking.
SL2.S2/S3: case files are short student summaries; waste audit data, shower flows and plan options are practice values; sorting answers follow common practice and local rules vary.

labs.outcome: Students investigate the role of scientific laws and theories and how they contribute to scientific knowledge.
labs.understanding: Scientific laws and theories play specific roles in describing and explaining phenomena.

K.text: Scientific knowledge can refer to facts, models, laws, and theories.
Observations that have been repeatedly confirmed may be accepted as scientific facts, which can be revised or rejected with additional evidence.

Scientific laws and theories are
• widely accepted
• supported by large bodies of evidence
• equally important
• used to make predictions about phenomena
• testable

Scientific laws
• are descriptions of phenomena
• can be expressed as a cause-and-effect relationship, rule, or an equation
• are considered universal
Scientific theories explain why or how phenomena occur and integrate a wide range of scientific knowledge.
A scientific model is a representation that helps explain or predict a phenomenon.
Scientists may use models to test hypotheses when developing scientific theories, such as the Big Bang theory.
Scientific theories cannot change into laws, and scientific laws cannot change into theories.

Science-related careers advance scientific knowledge by developing, testing, and applying scientific laws and theories in areas such as
• geology and resources, e.g., geophysicist
• sustainability, e.g., agronomist
• design criteria, e.g., instrumentation technician

S.text: Compare scientific laws to scientific theories.
Research a scientific law or theory.
Develop predictions for a phenomenon, using a scientific model.
Explore how a career in an applicable field of study in science uses the body of scientific knowledge.

labs.title: Laws and Theories Lab

labs.outcome: Students interpret patterns and possible bias in data.
labs.understanding: Unbiased data can help accurately predict trends.

K.text:
The relationship between two variables can reveal patterns to help
• predict trends
• identify risks
• make decisions
Critical-thinking skills can support the interpretation and analysis of patterns.

Bias can lead to incorrect conclusions due to
• errors in reasoning
• misinterpretation and inaccurate analysis of data
• flawed decision making

S.text: Analyze patterns in real-world situations.
Explore how bias can lead to incorrect conclusions.

labs.title: Patterns and Bias Lab

labs.unit: Matter: Atoms and the Periodic Table
labs.outcome: Students interpret matter in relation to atomic structure and physical and chemical properties.
labs.understanding: Atoms can be defined by their structure.

K.text: All matter is composed of atoms.
An atom is too small to be detected without the use of technology.

An atom is electrically neutral and is composed of subatomic particles, including
• protons, which have a positive charge
• electrons, which have a negative charge
• neutrons, which do not have a charge
Protons and neutrons make up an atom’s nucleus.
An atomic model is a theoretical representation of an atom’s structure.

Electrons can be represented as orbiting an atom’s nucleus in layered shells (Bohr model), including
• the first shell, which holds a maximum of two electrons
• the second shell, which holds a maximum of eight electrons
• the third shell, which holds a maximum of eight electrons

S.text: Model the location and charge of subatomic particles in an atom, limited to atoms that have a maximum of 18 electrons.
Research a technology used to study atoms and atomic structure.

labs.title: Atom Builder Lab
review: M1.K6: third shell taught as holding 8 for atoms up to 18 electrons; students told it can hold up to 18 in larger atoms.
M1.K6: 'orbiting' taught as the Bohr model's picture; the current electron cloud model (no fixed paths) is noted.
M1.K3: neutrality taught as equal protons and electrons; unbalanced particles named ions in passing; most hydrogen atoms have no neutrons.
M1.K1: taught as all ordinary matter; dark matter caveat kept to the teacher note.

labs.unit: Matter: Atoms and the Periodic Table
labs.outcome: Students interpret matter in relation to atomic structure and physical and chemical properties.
labs.understanding: Information about elements and their properties can be determined by using the periodic table.

K.text: Elements are pure substances made of only one type of atom and cannot be broken down into other substances by physical or chemical means.
An element is assigned a name and symbol.
All atoms of the same element have the same number of protons, which corresponds to that element’s atomic number.
The periodic table organizes elements according to atomic number and typically displays each element’s atomic mass and state of matter.

Elements in the periodic table are organized into
• groups, based on the number of electrons in each element’s outermost (valence) shell
• periods, based on each element’s number of electron shells
The organization of the periodic table can be used to distinguish metals from non-metals.

S.text: Research how the name and symbol of an element was assigned.
Determine the name, symbol, and properties of an element, using the periodic table.

labs.title: Periodic Table Lab
review: M2.K1: taught as written; nuclear reactions changing elements kept to the teacher note; one type of atom taught as same proton number, with different neutron numbers noted.
M2.K4: atomic mass taught as the average mass in u; bracketed values explained as longest-lasting isotope; state shown at room temperature, and unknown for elements 100 and up.
M2.K5: group rule taught for groups 1, 2 and 13 to 18 only; helium named as the exception; transition metals and the lower rows explained as not following a simple count; palladium's 4 shells noted.

labs.outcome: Students analyze the motion of objects resulting from interactions of forces, fluids, and pressure.
labs.understanding: The motion of an object changes because of forces acting on it.

K.text: Net force is the sum of all forces acting on an object.
When the net force on an object is zero the forces acting on it are balanced and the object’s motion will not change.
Changes in the speed and direction of an object’s motion are dependent on the net force.

Newton’s first law of motion, or the law of inertia, states that an object at rest stays at rest and an object in motion continues moving in a straight line at a constant speed unless acted upon by an unbalanced force.
The greater the mass of an object, the greater its inertia and the greater the force required to change the motion of the object.
Speed is the relationship between distance and time v = d/t

S.text: Describe how forces affect the motion of an object.
Predict the direction of an object’s motion based on net force, limited to horizontal motion.
Investigate how objects with different masses resist changes in motion when a force is applied.
Solve problems related to speed, distance, and time.
Conduct a controlled experiment to determine the relationship between speed, distance, and time.

labs.title: Forces in Motion Lab
review: F1.K2: 'motion will not change' taught as both cases (at rest stays at rest; moving keeps same speed and direction); misconception that balanced means still is named.
F1.K3/S2: net force kept to one horizontal line; sideways push in the motion map shows a direction change only; backward net force may stop then reverse the object.
F1.K4: inertia taught as a property, not a force; friction and air resistance named as the unbalanced forces that stop sliding objects; Principia date 1687 given as context.
F1.K5: mass separated from weight; equal-push data shows double mass gives half the speed change; F = ma not taught.
F1.K6: draft's v = d/t taught as average speed (no direction); 1 m/s = 3.6 km/h.

F1: toboggans described generally as developed by First Nations peoples for hauling loads over snow; please review wording. Surface slide distances, mover speeds and all Lab Bench data are estimates or invented practice data.

labs.outcome: Students analyze the motion of objects resulting from interactions of forces, fluids, and pressure.
labs.understanding: The motion and arrangement of particles can be used to predict the behaviour of fluids.

K.text: Fluids are substances that have no fixed shape and are capable of flowing, including liquids and gases.

Properties of fluids include
• pressure, which is the force exerted over an area
• viscosity, which is a fluid’s resistance to motion
• compressibility, which is how much a fluid’s volume changes in response to pressure
Pressure is created by particles colliding with a container’s wall as the wall exerts an equal but opposite force on the particles.
The space between particles affects the compressibility of a fluid.
Pascal’s law, named for a French scientist, expresses pressure as the force applied perpendicularly over an area P = F/A

Pascal’s law applies in technologies that use fluid to produce motion in systems, such as
• hospital beds
• automotive brakes
• jackhammers

S.text: Explain the relationship between pressure, force, and area.
Solve problems involving calculations related to pressure, force, and area.
Investigate the viscosity of various fluids.
Compare the compressibility of liquids and gases.
Apply the properties of fluids to move an object.

refs.title: Mix and Flow of Matter: Interactive Study Lab

labs.title: Fluids and Pressure Lab
review: F2.K2: viscosity taught as resistance to flowing (draft says 'resistance to motion'); a viscous fluid also resists objects moving through it; warming lowers viscosity for liquids only.
F2.K3: collision model taught with a gas; note added that liquid pressure also grows with depth from the weight of liquid above; temperature taught as harder, more frequent hits.
F2.K4: liquids taught as nearly incompressible; water about 0.005% per extra 100 kPa is a rounded reference value.

labs.outcome: Students examine the role of design criteria and testing in design processes.
labs.understanding: Design criteria and testing can help turn ideas into solutions.

K.text: Design criteria are the specific requirements a solution must meet to ensure needs, wants, or problems are addressed.
Constraints, e.g., budget or available resources, limit the design of a solution and can have positive or negative impacts on innovation.
Solutions can be tested to determine whether design criteria were met.
Data can be analyzed to identify potential strengths and weaknesses of a design.

S.text: Describe how constraints might impact a solution.
Design a test to evaluate potential solutions based on design criteria.
Analyze potential improvements to a solution.

labs.title: Design Criteria Lab
review: CS3.K1: must and want criteria added as a classroom extension (requirements and desirables); criteria taught as specific and measurable where possible.

CS3.K2: criteria and constraints overlap in practice (some sources list constraints as requirements); taught as a working distinction. Apollo 13 CO2 adapter (1970) used as a positive-impact example; please check wording.
CS3.K4: weighted decision matrix added beyond the statement; mean, targets and target direction used for analysis.
CS3: syringe hydraulic arm context borrowed from the fluids unit (force and distance trade-off, air compresses) stated qualitatively; all prices, trial data and scores are made up for practice.

labs.outcome: Students examine energy stores and transfers in an object or a system.
labs.understanding: Energy can be transferred between energy stores.

K.text: An energy store is a model to represent how much energy is available within a system.
Change in energy stores can indicate the amount of work done on an object or in a system.

Types of energy stores include
• thermal
• kinetic
• elastic
• gravitational
• chemical
• magnetic
• electrostatic
• nuclear

Energy is transferred from one energy store to another through a pathway, including
• heating
• radiation
• mechanical work
• electrical

S.text: Identify various types of energy stores.
Provide examples of energy stores.
Describe how energy is transferred between energy stores through energy pathways.

labs.title: Energy Stores Lab
review: EN1.K1: 'available' taught as how much energy a system has and where; stores are a bookkeeping model, and energy spread into the surroundings' thermal store is still there but hard to use.

EN1.K2: store change equals work done only for transfers by a force (hoist at steady speed); heating and radiation change stores without work. W = F × d from Science 7 F2; mgh and ½mv² shown as context only (g = 9.8 N/kg).
EN1.K3: chemical store taught as fuel or food together with oxygen; nuclear store named only (Sun fusion, uranium fission); gravitational store noted as belonging to object and Earth.

EN1.K4: heating taught as conduction and convection, radiation as its own wave pathway (light, infrared; sound often grouped here), unlike Science 7 EN2 which listed radiation under heating; light, sound and electricity taught as pathways, not stores.

EN1: toboggan values, hoist loads, ramp data (about 3%, 12%, 30% friction losses) and practice problems are made up and labelled; Bow River hydro, southern Alberta wind and Edmonton LRT are general contexts.

labs.outcome: Students examine energy stores and transfers in an object or a system.
labs.understanding: Static electricity accumulates and can be discharged, which results in the transfer of energy.

K.text:
Static electricity, or electrostatic charge, is the accumulation of electrons on the surface of a material and is used in equipment such as
• laser printers
• paint sprayers
• air filters

Static electricity can occur when two objects are rubbed together, which transfers electrons from the surface of one material to the other and causes
• the material that loses electrons to become positively charged
• the material that gains electrons to become negatively charged

When charged materials interact,
• like charges repel
• unlike charges attract
• charged objects are attracted to neutral objects (induction)
Static electricity is often discharged from the surface of a material in the form of a spark when a conductor touches the material.
Static electricity can cause natural phenomena, including lightning.

S.text: Explain how static electricity is discharged through the transfer of electrons.
Investigate how charged materials interact with one another.
Research how lightning results from static electricity in clouds.

labs.title: Static Charge Lab
review: EN2.K1: static electricity taught as a charge imbalance on a surface (extra electrons negative, missing electrons positive), not only an accumulation of electrons; laser printer, paint sprayer and air filter steps are simplified.

EN2.K2: rubbing taught as contact and separation that moves electrons, charge conserved; the 13-material rubbing series is a common classroom order that varies by source and humidity; carpet charging modelled as the person gaining electrons.
EN2.K3: attraction to neutral objects taught as induced charge separation (electrons move in conductors, shift within atoms in insulators, polarization named once); object stays neutral overall.
EN2.K4: spark taught as jumping a small air gap just before contact; quiet discharge through humid air and grounding added; gas station touch-metal-first advice needs a wording check.

EN2.K5/S3: ice crystal and graupel collision model (leading explanation, still researched); lightning about 30 000 °C (sources 20 000 to 30 000 °C); flash to bang 340 m/s, about 3 s per km; indoors-when-thunder-roars and 30 minute rule need a check against ECCC wording.
EN2: electron counts, carpet charge units, spark gaps and tape test outcomes are made-up practice values; lightning flagged as a possibly sensitive topic.

labs.outcome: Students examine energy stores and transfers in an object or a system.
labs.understanding: Energy can be transferred as a wave.

K.text: A wave is a disturbance or oscillation that transfers energy from one point to another without transporting matter, e.g., a wave on a string.

Waves have a repeating pattern and measurable properties, including
• wavelength
• frequency
• amplitude
• period
• speed
Waves with higher frequency and higher amplitude transfer a greater amount of energy from one energy store to another.

Waves can be classified by type, depending on whether they require a medium to propagate, for example:
• mechanical waves, such as seismic and water, require a medium
• electromagnetic waves, such as radio and microwave, do not require a medium
Mechanical waves oscillate the particles of a medium while transferring energy in the direction the wave travels.

When a wave encounters a new medium, the wave can be
• transmitted
• reflected
• refracted
• dispersed
• absorbed
The law of reflection states that when a wave strikes a surface, the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection.
Refraction is the bending of a wave due to a change in speed when the wave passes through a new medium.

S.text: Relate energy stores and transfers to waves.
Describe the properties of a wave.
Differentiate between mechanical and electromagnetic waves.
Interpret the behaviour of waves when encountering different surfaces or mediums.
Represent the law of reflection.

labs.title: Wave Energy Lab
review: EN3.K3: 'higher frequency and amplitude transfer more energy' taught as energy carried each second for the same wave type and medium (energy ∝ A² × f² as context); light noted as packet energy set by frequency, brightness by number of packets.
EN3.K4: 'do not require a medium' taught as can cross empty space; EM waves can also pass through some materials; Sun distance and light time rounded (150 million km, about 8 min).
EN3.K5: transverse and longitudinal added as brief context for the two directions particles oscillate; P and S waves described qualitatively (P faster), no speeds.
EN3.K6: 'dispersed' is ambiguous; taught as a mix of frequencies spreading apart because each travels at a slightly different speed (prism, rainbow); scattering only mentioned under reflection.

EN3.K7/K8: angles measured from the normal (practice converts angles from the surface); refraction taught as bending when entering at an angle, no bending along the normal; light speeds rounded (300 000, 225 000, 200 000 km/s).

EN3: sound speeds rounded (343 m/s air at 20 °C, 1480 m/s water); Sylvan Lake wave values, ripple tank energies and echo times are made-up practice data; earthquakes flagged as a possibly sensitive topic in deck notes.

labs.unit: Life Science: Cells and Organ Systems
labs.outcome: Students analyze the structures and functions of cells and organ systems.
labs.understanding: Cells support life in organisms of varying complexity.

K.text: Cells are the basic unit of life and vary in size, shape, and function.
Microscopes have enabled and advanced the study of cells.
The total magnification of a compound light microscope is the product of the magnification power of the microscope’s lenses.
Organelles are specialized structures that support specific functions within the cells of unicellular and multicellular organisms.

Organelles found in both plant and animal cells include
• cell membrane
• nucleus
• cytoplasm
• mitochondria
• ribosomes
• vacuoles
Organelles found only in plant cells include the cell wall and chloroplasts.
Some unicellular organisms, including bacteria, have no nucleus.
Some unicellular organisms, such as bacteria, fungi, and protists, can affect the health of humans and other multicellular organisms.

Processes that regulate the internal environment of a cell include
• cellular respiration, which provides energy
• diffusion, which enables movement of vital substances
• osmosis, which enables movement of water
• protein formation, which supports specific functions
The semi-permeable membrane of the cell enables diffusion and osmosis.

S.text: Use a microscope to study cells.
Calculate total magnification of a microscope.
Create diagrams of cells based on a microscope image.
Identify organelles in plant and animal cells.
Describe the function of organelles.
Research how a unicellular organism can affect the health of another organism.
Investigate the processes of diffusion and osmosis.
Describe processes that regulate the internal environment of cells.

labs.title: Cell Explorer Lab
review: LS1.K2: cell theory added as context; timeline dates (Hooke 1665, van Leeuwenhoek 1670s, Schleiden 1838, Schwann 1839, Remak and Virchow 1850s, Ruska and Knoll 1931, University of Toronto electron microscope 1938) need a check.
LS1.K3: lens values (10× eyepiece; 4×, 10×, 40× objectives) and fields of view (about 4.5, 1.8 and 0.45 mm) are typical values that vary by microscope; cell size estimate from field of view added.

LS1.K6: 'only in plant cells' taught as not in animal cells; fungi and bacteria also have walls, algae have chloroplasts, and root or bulb cells have no chloroplasts.
LS1.K7: taught as all bacteria lacking a nucleus (DNA loop in cytoplasm); yeasts and protists noted as unicellular with a nucleus; mature red blood cells appear once as a Sort It challenge card.

LS1.K8: fungi taught through unicellular yeasts; most microbes described as harmless or helpful; clubroot described as a protist-like soil parasite; Alberta details (clubroot in canola since the early 2000s, Giardia in untreated water) need a check; disease content is general science, not medical advice.
LS1.K9: respiration taught as a word equation in the mitochondria; protein formation at ribosomes using instructions from the nucleus (DNA left for LS2).
LS1.K10: semi-permeable noted as also called selectively permeable; osmosis defined toward the side with more dissolved particles; particle model uses simple gaps (transport proteins mentioned only).

labs.outcome: Students analyze the structures and functions of cells and organ systems.
labs.understanding: Cell division is essential for survival and diversity.

K.text: Deoxyribonucleic acid, or DNA, is the genetic information that provides instructions necessary for survival of the cell.
Most animal and plant cells store DNA in the nucleus, while cells without a nucleus, such as bacterial cells, may store DNA in the cytoplasm.
Cells within an individual organism contain the same DNA.

Cell division enables
• growth
• repair
• reproduction
• variation
Mitosis is a type of cell division that creates two identical daughter cells and enables growth and repair.
Meiosis is a type of cell division that creates four non-identical daughter cells, which are used in sexual reproduction.

S.text: Compare the location of DNA in different types of cells.
Identify the type of cell division from a given representation.
Compare mitosis and meiosis.

labs.outcome: Students analyze the structures and functions of cells and organ systems.
labs.understanding: The interdependent functions of organ systems influence the overall health of an individual.

Complex organisms, exhibit increasing levels of structural organization, including
• cell
• tissue
• organ
• organ systems
• organism
Specialized cells, such as nerve cells and red blood cells, perform specific functions.
Stem cells are non-specialized cells that can specialize into any type of cell.

Organ systems in humans are interdependent and include
• digestive
• respiratory
• circulatory
• muscular
• skeletal
• nervous
• excretory
Diagnostic medical procedures, such as X-rays and blood tests, can be used to identify function level or diseases in organ systems.

labs.outcome: Students examine ways to improve efficiency in computer systems.
labs.understanding: Programs can be enhanced for efficiency.

K.text: Functions can be designed in a programming language.
An event can be a detectable action, change, or occurrence.

A program recognizes and can respond to an event, including an
• external event, e.g., mouse click
• internal event, e.g., a timer or count is completed
Sensors are devices that collect data from the environment for input to the IPO cycle and can be used in many applications, such as robotics.
Variables store information that can be retrieved and changed throughout a program.
Variables are given a descriptive name and are assigned in different ways, including as a numerical value or a string of text.

A variable can be used with
• loops
• conditionals
• functions
• events
Efficient code uses functions, variables, and events effectively to ensure programs run faster and more reliably, enhancing task performance.

labs.outcome: Students examine ways to improve efficiency in computer systems.
labs.understanding: AI impacts human tasks in a variety of ways.

AI systems can increase efficiency by facilitating
• information processing
• decision making
• task completion

Types of machine learning include
• supervised learning, where labelled examples are provided
• unsupervised learning, where AI finds patterns in data without labelled examples
• reinforcement learning, where AI improves through trial and error with rewards and penalties

Bias in a machine that uses AI can be introduced by
• developers
• data sets
• algorithms
• user input
Generative AI can produce digital content such as images, text, videos, and music.
A chatbot can simulate conversations with online users, understand questions, and give answers in real time, by using AI.
Recommendation algorithms are AI programs that predict content an individual may like based on that individual’s previous online activity.

Scientists leverage AI in a variety of ways, such as
• data analysis
• climate modelling
• classifying galaxies in space images
AI can impact jobs by automating repetitive tasks, providing new career opportunities, and changing the skills needed for future work.

The use of AI has ethical implications, such as
• privacy and security
• fairness and bias
• misinformation and deepfakes
• decision making and accountability
• the influence of algorithm output on user behaviour

Explore AI, considering ethics and bias.

Examine ways AI is reshaping the workforce.

labs.outcome: Students investigate Earth’s geological history and its implications for resource exploration.
labs.understanding: Evidence from geological records provides information about Earth’s history.

K.text:
The geological time scale organizes Earth’s history into time intervals and is used to represent
• timing of major geological events
• the appearance and disappearance of life forms
Relative dating is a technique used to determine younger and older rock layers.

The fossil record provides information about Earth’s history, including
• geological events
• past climates and environments
• living and extinct organisms
Fossils are found in sedimentary rocks and are formed over thousands to millions of years under specific conditions.
Fossils are formed when remains or impressions of a once-living organism are mineralized or compressed.
Evidence of change over time can be found by comparing organisms and fossils.
Remains and impressions of once-living organisms can be destroyed by geological processes.
The badlands in what is now Alberta were referred to by early French explorers as “les mauvaises terres à traverser,” or bad lands to cross, and are renowned for extensive fossil beds.

Distinguish between younger and older rock layers.
Explore how different types of fossils are formed.

labs.outcome: Students investigate Earth’s geological history and its implications for resource exploration.
labs.understanding: Geological resource extraction methods change Earth’s surface.

K.text: Geological resources are naturally occurring materials found on or below Earth's surface that have economic value and can be extracted for human use.
Geological resources are unevenly distributed across Earth due to past geological processes.

Alberta’s geological resources, including fossil fuels and minerals, provide the raw materials that can be used to produce plastics and other components found in products such as medical devices and cell phones.
Humans change Earth’s surface by extracting materials such as coal and gravel from surface mines, and materials such as copper and iron from underground mines.
Many methods are used to locate and identify geological resources, e.g., surveying Earth’s surface and core sample drilling.

In Alberta, responsible resource extraction reduces environmental impacts and involves activities such as
• carbon capture and storage
• methane emission reduction
• water recycling and filtration
• tailings management

Analyze potential economic and environmental impacts of geological resource extraction.

labs.outcome: Students analyze the origin and evolution of the universe.
labs.understanding: Understandings of the universe have changed over time.

K.text: Astronomy is the scientific study of the universe.
Our solar system is part of the Milky Way galaxy, which is one of billions of galaxies in the universe.
Almost all stars that can be seen with the naked eye are part of the Milky Way.

Understandings, theories, and models of the universe and our solar system have evolved throughout history, such as those developed by
• ancient civilizations, e.g., Babylonia and ancient Greece
• mathematicians and astronomers, e.g., Ptolemy, and Galileo
The Big Bang theory explains the origin of the universe as starting from a dense, single point state that expanded under high temperature and pressure.
As the universe expanded and cooled, hydrogen and helium formed, leading to the first stars, the creation of heavier elements, and eventually the solar system.
The brightness of a star as observed from Earth depends on the star’s luminosity and distance from Earth.

Stars have a life cycle that includes
• formation
• changes in mass, size, and brightness
• star death

Explore how understandings, theories, and models of the universe have changed over time.
Describe the origin and evolution of the universe according to the Big Bang theory.

labs.outcome: Students examine how sustainability supports the needs of future generations.
labs.understanding: Sustainability supports present needs while addressing long-term impacts.

K.text: Environmental stewardship can support sustainability by meeting present needs in ways that also consider the needs of future generations.
Sustainability refers to the ability of systems to function effectively into the future.

Actions that support sustainability include
• using green technology
• managing resources while protecting air, land, and water quality
• planning urban or rural expansion while preserving natural areas
• setting targets for reducing pollution, waste, and greenhouse gas emissions
Green technology, such as electric or hydrogen-powered vehicles, solar power, carbon capture and storage, and vertical farming, can reduce impacts of human activity on the environment.
Technologies, including AI and drones, can be leveraged to reduce environmental impacts by monitoring, predicting, and improving how resources are used.
Sustainable agriculture protects biodiversity, supports soil and ecosystem health, and maximizes long-term yield.
Sustainability initiatives have led to innovations such as precision agriculture and autonomous zero-emission mining equipment.
Cleaner energy resources, such as natural gas, hydrogen, nuclear, and renewables, can help balance energy demands with sustainability goals by reducing greenhouse gas emissions.
Hydrogen can be used in gas utility systems, transportation, industrial processes, power generation, and power storage.
Alberta has uranium resources available for use as part of a clean energy strategy that includes nuclear energy.
Sustainability efforts can have social, environmental, and economic impacts.

S.text: Relate environmental stewardship to sustainability.
Explain actions that support sustainability.
Investigate ways in which technologies can be used to enhance sustainability.
Explore ways in which energy resources can be used to support sustainable energy in Alberta.

labs.outcome: Students relate understandings of phenomena to scientific theories.
labs.understanding: Understandings of phenomena can change over time.

K.text: When multiple scientific explanations of phenomena appear to be valid, new evidence is needed.
Accepted scientific theories are the simplest, most supported, and most comprehensive explanations of phenomena.

Peer review confirms the validity of scientific work, e.g., scientific theories, and includes
• examination of investigation techniques
• analysis and interpretation of data
New technologies and methods can reveal new evidence that can lead to a scientific theory or model being changed.

If substantial contradictory evidence is collected over time, a scientific theory can be
• restricted to a specific range of conditions
• revised to include the new evidence
• replaced with a new theory

Science-related careers apply knowledge of phenomena in areas such as
• electricity, e.g., electrician
• agriculture, e.g., agricultural engineer
• space exploration, e.g., space lawyer
• innovation, e.g., hydrogen systems technician

labs.title: Theory Shift Lab

labs.outcome: Students analyze claims and data for bias.
labs.understanding: Biased or selective data undermines scientific understandings.

K.text: Survivorship bias occurs when attention is placed on successful outcomes because they are visible and easier to evaluate, while failures are ignored or overlooked due to lack of visibility.
Claims that are presented as scientific but do not align with available evidence or are based on biased treatment of data are not accepted by the scientific community.
Data and evidence can be represented in ways that appear to support unscientific claims, including reporting influenced by selection bias or the use of an inappropriate scale.
Selection bias occurs when research participants or data are not randomly selected.
Critical-thinking skills can be used to analyze claims.

S.text: Describe how survivorship bias and selection bias could lead to misleading or inaccurate conclusions.
Interpret data for evidence of survivorship bias and selection bias.
Differentiate between scientific theories and unscientific claims.

labs.title: Claim Check Lab

labs.outcome: Students examine how variation occurs in organisms and species.
labs.understanding: Genetic traits of organisms are determined by DNA.

K.text:
DNA contains the genetic code of an organism needed
• to make each type of organism
• to make each type of cell in an organism
• for cell growth and repair
• for cell reproduction
A sequence of DNA can be used to identify species and individual organisms, except for identical twins, in which DNA sequences are nearly identical.
DNA is a double helix structure and can be organized into chromosomes.
Human cells typically contain 23 pairs of chromosomes.
Chromosomes contain segments of DNA, called genes, which control the formation of proteins that affect the genetic traits of an organism.
Alleles are different forms of the same gene that result in variations of a trait.
Mutations are changes in a DNA sequence that can occur naturally during cell division or due to environmental factors and can be advantageous, harmful, or neutral.
Mutations in sex cells may result in new genetic traits that can be inherited by offspring, while mutations in body cells are not inherited and may lead to diseases.

S.text: Describe the structure and function of DNA.
Model the structure of DNA.
Explain the relationship between DNA, genes, chromosomes, and genetic traits of organisms.
Research an example of a genetic mutation.

labs.title: Variation and Inheritance Lab
