labs.outcome: Students examine how variation occurs in organisms and species.
labs.understanding: Genetic variation can lead to evolutionary change in populations.

K.text: Reproduction is a biological process through which organisms transmit DNA to produce offspring.
Asexual reproduction is an efficient way to produce new individuals that receive their genetic material from a single parent, through processes such as binary fission and budding.
In sexual reproduction, each parent contributes one chromosome from each of their chromosome pairs to their offspring.

Sexual reproduction results in greater genetic variation than asexual reproduction due to the mixing of DNA from two different parents during meiosis, while asexual reproduction relies mainly on mutations for genetic variation.
Genetic variation refers to the differences in DNA among individuals within a population or species.
Variation can be caused by differences in genetic material, environmental factors, or both.
Adaptations are genetic traits that provide survival and reproductive advantages.
Natural selection is the process by which adaptations become more common in future generations.
Evolution is the change in a population over generations through natural selection and does not occur within an individual’s lifetime.
Theories of natural selection and evolution are based upon Darwin’s observations and ideas.
Artificial selection is a process used by humans to selectively breed organisms for desired genetic traits and is used in agricultural products such as canola.

S.text: Compare sexual and asexual reproduction.
Research species that reproduce asexually, sexually, or both.
Describe the relationships among genetic variation, adaptation, natural selection, and evolution.
Discuss Darwin’s contribution to the theory of evolution.
Research examples of artificial selection used to develop agricultural products, including those used in Alberta.

labs.title: Variation and Inheritance Lab
labs.note: Built earlier from this draft. Covers LS1 to LS3 together.

labs.outcome: Students examine how variation occurs in organisms and species.
labs.understanding: Genetic inheritance can be used to predict traits from one generation to the next.

K.text: Genetic material, passed down through sexual reproduction to offspring, results in traits that can be the same as, different from, or a blend of the traits of both parents.
Single gene inheritance describes traits determined by the combination of alleles of one gene.

Alleles can be either dominant or recessive and the combination determines the trait that is expressed when
• at least one copy of the dominant allele is present, resulting in a dominant trait
• two copies of the recessive allele are present, resulting in a recessive trait
A Punnett square can be used to represent genetic crosses.
Genotype is the set of alleles that determines an organism’s traits, and phenotype is the observable traits of an organism.
Most genetic traits are complex, such as hair colour and eye colour, and are the result of the interaction of multiple different genes.
Discrete variation is expressed as distinct versions of the same trait, e.g., blood type, and continuous variation in traits is expressed on a spectrum, e.g., height.

The field of genetics involves ethical issues, such as
• DNA modification
• ownership of genetic information
• consent and sharing of DNA profiles

S.text: Discuss variation in phenotypes observed in plants and animals, including humans.
Distinguish between genotype and phenotype.
Represent single gene inheritance in a genetic cross.
Determine phenotype from a given genotype.
Distinguish between discrete and continuous traits.
Consider implications of an ethical issue related to genetics.

labs.outcome: Students investigate geological processes related to the movement of tectonic plates.
labs.understanding: The layers of Earth behave differently and contribute to geological processes that continually reshape Earth’s surface.

K.text:
Layers of Earth include
• the crust: the thin outermost layer of continental and oceanic rock
• the mantle: the thickest and mostly solid layer between the crust and core
• the core: the innermost layer with a fluid outer core and solid inner core
The lithosphere consists of large tectonic plates that make up Earth’s crust and the uppermost solid part of Earth’s mantle.
Tectonic plates move on the upper part of the mantle because of convection currents and gravitational forces.
The theory of continental drift states that Earth’s continents were once a large land mass that broke and drifted apart over millions of years.
The theory of continental drift is supported by evidence, including the shapes of Earth’s continents and similarities among fossils found on different continents.

The theory of plate tectonics builds on the theory of continental drift and describes Earth’s crust as seven primary tectonic plates that move over Earth’s upper mantle, driven by heat-related convection.

Tectonic plates are classified as
• oceanic, which are thinner and denser than continental plates
• continental, which are thicker and less dense than oceanic plates

Evidence supporting the theory of plate tectonics includes
• seafloor spreading
• mountain formation
• seismic activity
• volcanic activity
The Rocky Mountains were formed by the collision and compression of tectonic plates.

S.text: Model Earth’s layers.
Relate the theory of continental drift to the theory of plate tectonics.
Discuss how the movement of tectonic plates changes Earth’s surface.

labs.outcome: Students investigate geological processes related to the movement of tectonic plates.
labs.understanding: Various geological hazards are associated with geological processes within Earth.

K.text:
Regions around the Ring of Fire, including the west coast of Canada, have high exposure to geological hazards that include
• volcanic activity
• earthquakes
• landslides
• tsunamis

Historical accounts can support scientific understandings of geological events, such as the
• Cascadia earthquake
• Frank Slide
• Tseax Cone eruption

Geological hazards can be monitored and their impacts minimized in a variety of ways, such as
• early warning systems and emergency preparedness
• construction standards and land-use planning
• seismographic detection and gas emission monitoring
The Modified Mercalli Intensity scale and the Richter scale are used to measure the intensity of earthquakes.

labs.outcome: Students investigate the composition and chemical interactions of elements and compounds.
labs.understanding: Pure substances can be classified by their composition.

K.text: Pure substances can be classified as elements or compounds.

An element can be
• monoatomic: composed of a single atom of the same type, e.g., Rn
• diatomic: composed of two atoms of the same type, e.g., H2
• polyatomic: composed of more than two atoms of the same type, e.g., S8
A molecule is a group of atoms that act as a single unit and can range in size, e.g., O2, CO2, DNA.
A compound can be classified as ionic or molecular.
An ionic compound is composed of oppositely charged ions, which combine in specific ratios resulting in a neutral charge.
The ratio of atoms in an ionic compound can be determined by using the periodic table.

An atom that has gained one or more electrons is a negatively charged ion, referred to as an anion, and an atom that has lost one or more electrons is a positively charged ion, referred to as a cation.
A molecular compound is composed of two or more non-metal atoms that share electrons.
Rules for naming ionic and molecular compounds are established by the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry, or IUPAC.
The IUPAC chemical formula for a compound uses the symbol for each element and shows each element’s number of atoms in subscript, if that number is greater than one.
Hazards of pure substances can be identified by using the Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System, or WHMIS.

S.text: Identify monoatomic, diatomic, and polyatomic elements.
Model structures of elements and compounds.
Explain relationships between atoms, elements, ions, molecules, and compounds.
Name compounds composed of two elements when given the chemical formula.
Determine the chemical formula of a compound composed of two elements when given the IUPAC name.
Determine the number of atoms of each element in ionic or molecular compounds.
Identify the hazards represented by WHMIS pictograms.

labs.outcome: Students investigate the composition and chemical interactions of elements and compounds.
labs.understanding: Chemical reactions of pure substances can be determined by observable and quantifiable changes.

K.text: A chemical reaction is a process in which the atoms that make up the original substances, or reactants, regroup into new substances or products.
Matter is not created or destroyed during a chemical reaction; therefore, the mass of the reactants is equal to the mass of the products.

Observable evidence of chemical change includes
• change in colour or odour
• production of gas or precipitate
• change in energy, e.g., production of light or change in temperature
Physical change, such as melting an ice cube or dissolving sugar in water, does not result in new products.
The reactivity of a pure substance depends on the number of electrons in the substance’s outermost (valence) shell.
Atoms are more stable when their outermost (valence) electron shell is full.
Chemical reactions can be represented in various ways, including with chemical equations and by modelling.
The rate of chemical reactions is affected by factors, such as temperature and concentration, that influence how often particles collide.
WHMIS and other safety protocols need to be considered when working with chemicals.

S.text: Perform chemical reactions, using a variety of reactants, to demonstrate chemical change.
Differentiate between physical and chemical change.
Perform a chemical reaction to demonstrate how mass is conserved.
Discuss WHMIS and other safety protocols.
Represent chemical reactions as chemical equations.
Demonstrate chemical reactions, using models.
Explain the role of electrons in reactivity of pure substances.

labs.outcome: Students examine electric current and conservation of energy.
labs.understanding: Energy can be transferred by a current within a circuit.

K.text: Electric current is a transfer of energy through the flow of electrons in a conductor.
The rate at which a charge passes a given point in a circuit is expressed in amperes, named after a French physicist (André-Marie Ampère).
A circuit is created when current flows continuously through a closed path.
Potential difference, or voltage, expressed in volts, causes current to flow because of a difference in electric charge between two points along a circuit.

The main components that can make up a circuit include
• an energy store, e.g., a battery or cell
• a conductor
• a load device, which transfers energy into another energy store, e.g., a light bulb
• a control device, e.g., a switch or a resistor
Components of circuits can be arranged in series or in parallel and can be represented with schematic diagrams that use component symbols.

In a series circuit, current
• flows along a single path
• is the same at any point in the circuit

In a parallel circuit,
• current flows along multiple paths
• the total current is equal to the sum of the current in the branches
• not every branch needs to be closed for the circuit to function
• voltage in each branch is the same
Conventional current, defined as the direction in which a positive charge would flow, was established before the discovery of electrons.
Technologies used to measure voltage, current, and resistance include voltmeters, ammeters, and multimeters.
Conductors, such as copper, aluminium, and tap water, are materials that allow a charge to be transferred.
Insulators, such as rubber, wood, and deionized water, are materials that impede the transfer of a charge.
Resistance, expressed in ohms, is a measure of how much a circuit component reduces current.
Properties of conductors, such as material, length, and cross-sectional area, affect resistance.
Resistors can be used to control current in devices.
Ohm’s law expresses the relationship between voltage, current, and resistance V =I×R.
Safe practices are required when handling or near electric current.

S.text: Design schematic diagrams of series and parallel circuits.
Investigate the use of control devices to manage the flow of electric current.
Measure voltage, current, and resistance in circuits.
Compare the characteristics of series and parallel circuits.
Troubleshoot series and parallel circuits.
Explain the relationship between voltage, current, and resistance.
Apply Ohm’s law to solve problems involving calculations related to voltage, current, and resistance.
Identify safe and unsafe practices around electric current.

labs.outcome: Students examine electric current and conservation of energy.
labs.understanding: The conservation of energy is evident in the energy transfers of electrical devices.

K.text: Power, expressed in watts, is the rate at which an electrical device transfers energy.
The power rating can be used to calculate the energy input required by a device.
The relationship between power and time can be used to determine energy input E = P × t.

The law of conservation of energy states that energy
• cannot be created or destroyed
• can be transferred from one energy store to another
During an energy transfer, energy dissipates from a system through heating the system’s surroundings, reducing the amount of useful energy available.
The energy efficiency of electrical devices can be determined by comparing the input from the energy store to the output of the device, quantified in a ratio.
Appliances or devices can be rated according to their energy efficiency by programs such as EnerGuide or Energy Star.
The cost of operating electrical devices is the product of the energy rating in kilowatt hours and the price of power per kilowatt hour.
In Alberta, electricity can be derived from various sources, including oil, natural gas, coal, biomass, solar radiation, and wind.

S.text: Explain the relationships between power, energy, and efficiency.
Solve problems involving energy, power, and time.
Apply the law of conservation of energy to account for the total energy involved in energy transfers.
Relate energy efficiency to energy stores and transfers.
Solve problems involving the efficiency of various electrical devices.
Solve problems involving the cost of operating electrical devices.
Explore sources of electricity in Alberta.

labs.outcome: Students examine text-based programming languages.
labs.understanding: Text-based programming languages can enable computers to perform more complex tasks.

K.text: Text-based programming languages use words, phrases, numbers, and keyboard symbols to communicate instructions instead of the shapes and blocks that are used in visual block-based programming.
Text-based programming languages provide greater control over how programs can be designed.

Key features of text-based programming languages are
• syntax
• structure
• complexity
Each text-based programming language has its own syntax, a set of rules that governs the arrangement and combination of symbols to create a program.
Pseudocode is a step-by-step description of an algorithm that resembles the structure of a programming language.

S.text: Compare sequences of visual block-based code to the same sequences expressed in various text-based programming languages.
Convert a sequence of visual block-based code to a text-based programming language.

labs.outcome: Students examine how design processes can result in innovative solutions.
labs.understanding: Innovation stems from creativity when developing and implementing solutions.

K.text: Design processes lead to innovations when new or improved solutions are implemented.

Innovation involves approaching design processes with the intent of
• exploring new or improved ways to address needs, wants, or problems
• creating solutions that add value
• taking risks
Responsible innovation considers positive and negative potential impacts of solutions.

labs.outcome: Students investigate energy transfers in relation to sound waves and light waves.
labs.understanding: Sound waves transfer energy from the source of the sound wave and behave predictably.

K.text:
Sound waves are mechanical waves that
• require a vibrating source
• require a medium to propagate
• travel in straight lines
• travel in all directions from the source
The frequency of a sound wave determines the pitch, and the amplitude of a sound wave determines the volume.
The speed of a sound wave depends on the temperature and type of medium through which the wave travels.

In most conditions, sound waves travel faster
• in higher temperatures
• through denser materials, e.g., sound travels faster through water than air

S.text: Describe how sound travels.
Identify different mediums through which sound waves can travel.
Compare pitch and volume, using sound-wave diagrams.
Explore scenarios that affect the speed of sound.

labs.outcome: Students investigate energy transfers in relation to sound waves and light waves.
labs.understanding: Light waves transfer energy from the source of the light wave.

K.text:
Light waves are electromagnetic waves that
• require a light source
• do not require a medium to propagate
• travel in straight lines
• travel in all directions from the source
The amplitude of a light wave determines brightness, and the frequency of a light wave determines colour.
Light waves behave differently when interacting with mediums of different transparency, e.g., transparent, translucent, or opaque.
The human eye can see only a portion of the electromagnetic spectrum, referred to as the visible light spectrum.
White light contains all colours of the visible light spectrum and can be dispersed through a prism.
Bodies can only be seen if they produce or reflect light.
A shadow is caused when light rays are absorbed by a body, creating an area of darkness behind the body.

S.text: Describe characteristics of light waves.
Investigate how light waves interact with different mediums.
Explore the effect of a prism on white light.
Discuss the formation of shadows in relation to the behaviour of light.

labs.outcome: Students investigate energy transfers in relation to sound waves and light waves.
labs.understanding: Optical technology uses the behaviour and interaction of light waves.

K.text:
Many technologies make use of the behaviour of light, such as
• optics and imaging
• medical applications
• security and sensors
Light travels in a straight line and can be represented by a light ray.
Mirrors reflect light, whereas lenses refract light.
Light interacts differently with mirrors and lenses, depending on the shape of the mirror or the lens.
The image of an object can change in size or orientation, depending on the object’s location relative to the mirror or lens.

S.text: Investigate a form of optical technology and how it is used.
Investigate how various shapes of mirrors and lenses produce different images.
Represent how light interacts with mirrors and lenses.
Explore the effect of the distance of an object from a mirror or lens on the image.

labs.outcome: Students examine opportunities for and implications of space exploration.
labs.understanding: The advancement of space exploration needs to ensure safety, sustainability, and equitable use.

K.text: Space exploration is enhanced by technology, including computers, rockets, telescopes, rovers, and space stations.
Canada makes contributions to space exploration, e.g., robotics and satellite technology.

Implications of space exploration include
• collection of data that could benefit life on Earth
• employment opportunities in the space industry
• long-term investment and maintenance costs
• space debris in orbit
• effects on the human body

International space law regulates space exploration through treaties to
• prohibit space appropriation
• promote peaceful exploration
• benefit humankind
• reduce contamination
Space exploration is advancing, and many aspects are not regulated by international space law.

Analyze implications of space exploration.
Discuss regulation of space exploration and consider what aspects are not regulated.

Research laboratories and human habitation on the Moon, Mars, or other celestial bodies could support space exploration in various ways, such as

labs.outcome: Students analyze climate change and other complex environmental issues in relation to sustainability.
labs.understanding: Complex environmental issues can be addressed by environmental stewardship and sustainability.

K.text:
Environmental stewardship and sustainability efforts can help address climate change and other complex environmental issues, such as
• plastic pollution
• resource scarcity, e.g., water and minerals
• food insecurity
• poor water and air quality
Monitoring water and air quality provides insight into pollution levels and supports informed decision making.
Climate change is accelerated by human activity and can be slowed by replacing or improving inefficient technologies and by transitioning to renewable and low-carbon energy resources.
Climate-smart agriculture increases productivity and efficiency, enhances resilience to climate change, and mitigates greenhouse gas emissions.

Advanced technologies and innovations can be leveraged to support climate-smart agriculture such as
• carbon capture and storage
• AI-powered monitoring
• smart irrigation
• greenhouse systems
Healthy soils store carbon and support the growth of nutrient dense crops.
Alberta is developing extraction methods for critical minerals, including lithium and uranium, which are in demand for clean energy technologies.

Sustainability can be supported by government actions, such as
• creating regulations for resource extraction
• setting pollution limits for industry
• offering incentives for developing or using eco-friendly technologies and transportation
Government environmental actions can gain public support through approaches such as educational campaigns or monetary incentives.
As the human population increases, the demand for resources increases and sustainability efforts become more important.
There are environmental considerations associated with AI and digital technologies.

S.text: Research a complex environmental issue, considering potential solutions.
Examine ways to slow the acceleration of climate change.
Explore government environmental actions.
Investigate critical minerals that support clean energy.
Connect environmental stewardship and sustainability efforts to demand for resources.
Discuss environmental considerations related to AI and digital technologies.
